scenes.narration: Two GPS questions hide inside "does this reaction work?" First: will this route actually reach the destination? That's thermodynamics — ΔG — and it tells you whether the reaction is favorable at all. Second: how congested is the road? That's kinetics — ΔG‡, the activation energy — and it tells you how fast you'll get there. Here's the line to remember: an enzyme answers only the second question. It never changes whether a reaction can happen, only how fast.
scenes.slideTitle: Thermodynamics vs. kinetics — a GPS analogy

scenes.narration: Map the sign of ΔG onto a traffic light. Green — ΔG less than zero — means go: the reaction is spontaneous. Yellow — ΔG equals zero — is equilibrium, no net movement. Red — ΔG greater than zero — means stop: the cell has to spend energy to push it forward. The crucial part is the caption: an enzyme cannot change the color of the light. It can only speed your passage through a green one. Spontaneity belongs to thermodynamics, not the catalyst.

A picture for the next section. Without an enzyme, reactants have to climb over a high mountain — the long way around. With an enzyme, they take a shortcut through a lower pass. Notice both routes end at the same place on the far side: the enzyme doesn't move the destination, it just makes the crossing easier. So how exactly does it lower the pass? That's the transition-state secret, coming up.

This is the single most important diagram in the chapter. Both curves start at the same substrate and end at the same product, so ΔG — the overall free-energy change — is identical with or without the enzyme. What changes is the height of the hill in between: the activation energy, ΔG‡, is far lower when the enzyme is present. Enzymes speed reactions by stabilizing the transition state at the top of that hill, not by changing where the reaction ends up.
scenes.slideTitle: Enzyme lowers activation energy, not ΔG

scenes.narration: The transition state is neither substrate nor product — it's a fleeting, highest-energy arrangement of atoms that exists for about ten femtoseconds. The top row shows the arc: substrate in, transition state, product out. The bottom row zooms in on the chemistry — bonds half-broken and half-formed at the same instant. The key insight: that transition state has a specific geometry, and it's the shape evolution has tuned the enzyme to recognize and grip.

Four panels, one idea. First, the enzyme lowers the activation barrier by releasing binding energy right at the transition state. Second, shape complementarity: the active site fits the transition state better than it fits the ground-state substrate. Third, the bookkeeping — catalyzed ΔG‡ equals the uncatalyzed barrier minus the binding energy. Fourth, the payoff in medicine: drugs shaped like the transition state exploit that tight fit, binding far harder than substrate mimics. The enzyme's job, in one line: bind the transition state tighter than the substrate.
